name: HSE incident and near-miss records
one_line: The record of an event in which a person was harmed or nearly was: the report of what happened, the investigation of why, the statements and scene evidence, the notification to a regulator, and the actions taken because of it. Its anchor is a dated event and a person's exposure to harm — not a product, a lot, an instrument or a purchase — and it is the one manufacturing situation whose principal sensitivity is a third party's health and identity rather than the holder's commercial secrets. Placeholder row written to J-DEPTH; fields: [] under PR-6.

deterministic: an injury or illness incident-report structure with labelled slots for the date and time of the event, the location or line, the task being performed at the time, what happened, the injury or illness and the affected body part, the treatment given, and whether the person returned to work; the co-occurrence of an event time, a person role and a harm description is the signal, never the word incident

a near-miss or hazard-observation structure with a labelled event identifier, the observed hazard or unsafe condition, an explicit no-injury or no-harm outcome, an immediate action taken, an owner and a closeout status — and carrying no product, lot, instrument, specification or measured-result slot at all

an incident-investigation structure joining a sequence-of-events narrative to a named causal method (a five-why chain, Ishikawa or fishbone cause categories, or an immediate-cause / underlying-cause / root-cause ladder) and a set of dated actions all tied to one incident identifier

a statutory injury log whose repeated rows carry case number, employee job title, date of the event, where the event occurred, description of injury or illness and body part, and mutually exclusive outcome columns for death, days away from work, job transfer or restriction, and other recordable cases, bounded to one establishment and one calendar year; the OSHA Form 300 Log of Work-Related Injuries and Illnesses is the named example and the OSHA Form 300A summary is its per-establishment annual total sheet

a regulator notification or submission acknowledgement naming an incident identifier, a reportable-event category and a submission reference — the RIDDOR F2508 online submission confirmation is the named example; the acknowledgement is a record of a notified event, not a purchase confirmation
a witness or operator statement: a first-person narrative of one dated event, the declarant's role at the time, a signature and date block, and a reference to an incident identifier

a signed attendance or acknowledgement sheet for a toolbox talk, safety stand-down or briefing whose subject names an incident identifier or the specific hazard the incident exposed, distinguishing it from a scheduled training record by that back-reference
an archive whose manifest links one incident identifier across a report, an investigation, statements, scene photographs and action records; the manifest is read without unpacking the archive to disk
needs_llm: an unlabelled shift-notebook page, handwritten near-miss card or scanned logbook where the harm, the event time and the location are only in prose or OCR
an email thread in which the harm description, the containment decision and the corrective action are distributed across replies with no labelled form anywhere in the bytes

deciding whether a photograph of a machine, guard or floor is incident-scene evidence or a routine maintenance, inspection or work-instruction illustration, when the only discriminator is surrounding or embedded text
separating an incident-triggered revision of a risk assessment or work instruction from a scheduled periodic review of the same document, where the two produce near-identical bytes
deciding whether a property-damage-only or dangerous-occurrence report belongs here or with an asset failure record, when no person is named as exposed
never_alone: the words incident, incident report, accident, near miss or investigation alone — information-technology, information-security, clinical, customer-service and insurance corpora all file documents carrying those exact words
a safety-sounding department, programme or organisation name alone (EHS, Health and Safety, Zero Harm, Safety Committee); an organisation name is never-alone evidence
a person's name alone in any role — the harmed party, a witness, the investigator or the approver; roles that share an entity type must be separated, not collapsed
an injury or body-part word appearing in free text, with no dated event structure around it
a bare date, a bare four-digit reference token, or a hazard word in a filename (guard, spill, fall, lockout, forklift) with no event structure
a safety data sheet, hazard pictogram, chemical name or exposure-limit table — these are reference material about a hazard, not a record that an event occurred
a photograph of a machine or a floor with no event anchor; and missing EXIF is not evidence that an image is scene documentation
a file extension, a folder path, or a shared download session

work_types: near-miss, hazard observation or unsafe-condition report
dangerous occurrence or property-damage-only event report
incident scene photograph, sketch or measurement record
statutory injury log or annual establishment summary
corrective or preventive action arising from an incident
safety alert, stand-down, toolbox talk or lessons-learned bulletin
incident-triggered revision of a risk assessment, permit or work instruction
return-to-work, restricted-duty or absence record arising from an event
grouping_reasons: an exact incident identifier shared between a report, an investigation, statements, photographs, a regulator acknowledgement and action records
an exact event date-time plus the same named location or line, where no incident identifier was ever issued (common for near-miss cards)
an archive or export manifest that already binds the members of one incident pack
an explicit back-reference from a safety alert, toolbox talk or revised risk assessment to one incident identifier

template.why: Empty by placeholder contract because the manufacturing schema declares no canonical fields. The recommendation held as prose is site, then the incident event, then record type — deliberately unlike the schema's default subject-first branches, because an HSE incident routinely has no product, no lot, no instrument and often no asset to sit under. This row is the one place in the schema where a calendar dimension has real evidence rather than convenience: the statutory injury log and its annual summary are per-establishment, per-calendar-year documents, so a year level under site is defensible for the log family specifically. It is still not recommended as the top level, because putting year first would scatter a single incident's report, statements, photographs and actions across calendar folders. No level is ever the harmed person, the witness or the investigator: 00 says the system 'should avoid using authorship or creator identity as a destination dimension' and that 'A folder should not become a collection point for everything produced by the same person or organization' — the same reasoning applies with more force to a person who is the subject of a harm record. Severity, recordability and reportability are judgements this catalogue must not make, so none of them is proposed as a dimension.

collides_with.signal: SAME FIXTURE BOTH SIDES: `CAPA-2026-012 effectiveness review.docx` opened in response to IR-2026-014 — this row owns the event record of harm to a person (event date-time, exposed person role, injury or no-injury outcome, witness statements, regulator notification), the neighbour owns the nonconformance and corrective-action workflow anchored on a product, lot, process or requirement (requirement-versus-observed condition, containment, disposition, effectiveness verification), discriminated by whether the subject of the harm is a person or an article: an injury, body-part, treatment or exposure slot supports this row, a specification, disposition or affected-lot slot supports the neighbour, and a file carrying both is two records in one packet rather than one row's evidence.

SAME FIXTURE BOTH SIDES: `Machine guarding risk assessment - Press 12 - rev C.pdf` reissued after IR-2026-014 — this row owns the retrospective record that an event occurred and what changed because of it, the neighbour owns the prospective demonstration that a plant, machine or process is acceptably safe (hazard identification, control hierarchy, residual-risk argument, revision control), discriminated by the presence of a dated event and an exposed person: a revision note back-referencing one incident identifier supports this row's pack membership, while the assessment's own hazard-and-control structure and revision history stay with the neighbour, and a scheduled periodic revision with no back-reference is the neighbour's alone.

SAME FIXTURE BOTH SIDES: `Spill report 2026-05-09 - coolant to surface drain.pdf` — this row owns the event where a person was harmed or exposed, the neighbour owns the release, emission, discharge or permit-limit exceedance measured against an environmental consent, discriminated by the receptor named in the report: a person, an injury or an exposure supports this row, a receiving medium, a consent or permit condition, a monitored limit or a notified environmental regulator supports the neighbour, and a spill that both injured an operator and breached a discharge consent is genuinely both and must not be silently assigned to one.

SAME FIXTURE BOTH SIDES: `Site safety inspection Plant 2.pdf` and an accident report bearing the identical form layout — this row owns events inside an operating plant with a controlled production line, process or machine, the neighbour owns events on a construction, refurbishment or property site under a professional instruction, discriminated by the surrounding operational anchor rather than by the form: a line, cell, production shift, process area or production asset supports this row, while a project or contract reference, a principal contractor or designer role, a work package, a subcontractor or a phase of construction supports the neighbour; a fit-out injury inside a factory building belongs to the neighbour despite the address.

SAME FIXTURE BOTH SIDES: `HSE risk register 2026 - Plant 2.xlsx` — this row owns the individual dated event and its investigation, the neighbour owns the standing management artefact of enumerated risks with owners, ratings, treatments and review dates, discriminated by whether the rows are events that happened or risks that might: a repeated event date, location and outcome per row supports this row (a statutory injury log is an event log, not a risk register), while a likelihood-and-impact grid, a treatment plan and a next-review date support the neighbour, and an incident that adds a register line does not convert the register into an incident record.

SAME FIXTURE BOTH SIDES: `Vehicle accident report VAN-14 2026-02-02.pdf` — this row owns events within a controlled plant boundary involving production work, the neighbour owns driver and vehicle events governed by transport rules (licence, tachograph or hours-of-service record, roadworthiness, roadside check, public-road collision), discriminated by where the event happened and what governs it: a line, process area or production asset supports this row, while a vehicle registration, driver licence reference, road location, third-party or police reference supports the neighbour; a forklift striking a pedestrian inside the plant is this row's, a delivery van collision on the road is not.

SAME FIXTURE BOTH SIDES: an occupational-health report or fitness-for-work assessment naming the person injured in IR-2026-014 — this row owns the employer-side record that an event occurred, held about a third party, the neighbour owns the corpus owner's own clinical record held by or for them, discriminated by whose corpus and whose body: a clinician-to-employer report with an employer addressee, an incident identifier and a restriction or fitness opinion supports this row's pack while carrying independent health evidence, whereas the same clinical letter in the injured person's own corpus, addressed to them, is the neighbour's; membership never converts a third party's health data into the holder's medical facts, and neither row may be used to route the other's file into a shallower privacy posture.

SAME FIXTURE BOTH SIDES: `Employers liability claim EL-88421 - IR-2026-014.pdf` — this row owns the operational record of the event and its investigation, the neighbour owns the policy and claim lifecycle (insurer, policy number, claim reference, claimant, reserve, settlement, renewal), discriminated by which slots carry the substance: an event narrative, causal analysis and corrective actions support this row, while a policy or claim reference, a reserve or settlement figure and an insurer or broker signatory support the neighbour, and a claim file's description-of-loss field is a cross-reference to an incident and never a replacement for the incident record.

falls_through_to.why: The principal fallback. Injury reports, statutory injury logs, witness statements, occupational-health correspondence and claim files name identified third parties and describe their bodies and treatment. 00 says Protected Records "may represent sensitive isolated material such as passport scans, medical documents, account statements, visas, legal forms, or credentials; it should normally remain local-only and must not cause filenames or content to be exposed in model prompts." That is the correct default posture for this row's core evidence, and it is a materially stricter fallback than the manufacturing schema's own residual set, which does not route to Protected Records at all.

00 says Independent Records "may live under Personal/Independent Records and hold standalone certificates, notices, confirmations, forms, and PDFs that have a durable purpose but no broader group." A de-identified near-miss card, a safety alert, a regulator acknowledgement or a blank incident form has durable purpose and names no one, so it does not need the protected posture and should not be pushed there merely for carrying the word incident.

00 says Review Later "may hold files whose meaning is partly understood but whose final location requires a future decision." An OCR-poor logbook page, an untitled investigation fragment, or a property-damage report with no named exposed person should abstain rather than manufacture an event, a site or a person role.

00 says Unsupported or Encrypted "may hold—or, more safely, represent without moving—password-protected archives, unreadable documents, damaged files, and unknown formats." An encrypted incident register or a proprietary EHS-system export must be represented without inferring a site, an event count or a sensitivity result from its filename.

sensitivity_why: This is the one manufacturing situation whose principal sensitivity is a third party's health and identity rather than the holder's commercial secrets. An injury report carries a named person, their job, their injury and affected body part, their treatment and treating facility; a statutory injury log carries many such people in one sheet; witness statements attribute conduct to named individuals; occupational-health correspondence is clinical. Commercial exposure is secondary but real, since incident and investigation files reveal plant layout, machine condition, staffing and control failures that also appear in claims and enforcement. The row assigns no handling class — that is P7's — and it must not infer recordability, reportability, severity, work-relatedness, fault, liability, fitness for work, or any retention or notification duty. Person names in every role stay search and privacy observations and never become destination dimensions.
open_question: NJ-HSE-1: the manufacturing schema proposes `quality_event` as its controlled-event key, and its own NJ-MFG-2 asks whether that should instead be a broader canonical `case`/`event`. This row is the concrete pressure on that question: a safety event is not a quality event, and forcing an injury under `quality_event` would misdescribe it, but minting a parallel `incident` key would fragment the same concept across schemas. Alternatives for R1c: (a) widen `quality_event` to any controlled event with an identifier and a closure state, (b) mint one shared `case` key and let each schema constrain its values, (c) keep them separate and accept two near-identical keys. NJ-HSE-2: whether an incident identifier may ever appear in a visible folder label, given that a branch named for one event, on a small site, can identify the person it happened to. NJ-HSE-3: whether the statutory-log family may carry a calendar-year dimension under site while the rest of the row stays event-anchored, or whether one row must have one dimension recommendation. NJ-HSE-4: whether third-party health data inside a business corpus needs a distinct privacy treatment from the holder's own health data, which `medical.personal-health-records` assumes.
